hints: Start by asking yourself, how much DNA can just ONE fork copy in the full 1 hour available? Remember to convert that hour into seconds first.
Now compare that one-fork total to the huge job of 150 million base pairs. Divide the total job by what one fork can do to find how many forks must work together.
walkthrough:
**Find what one fork can do in 1 hour**

Think of one replication fork as one worker. We need to know how much work one worker can finish in the time allowed.

First convert time:
$$1 \text{ hour} = 60 \times 60 = 3600 \text{ s}$$

Then multiply by the rate:
$$50 \text{ base pairs per second} \times 3600 \text{ s} = 180,000 \text{ base pairs per fork}$$

**Find how many forks are needed for the whole chromosome**

One fork only copies about 180,000 base pairs, but the chromosome has about 150,000,000 base pairs. So many forks must work at the same time.

Use this simple idea:
$$\text{number of forks} = \frac{\text{total DNA}}{\text{DNA per fork}}$$
$$\text{number of forks} = \frac{150,000,000}{180,000} \approx 833$$

**Pick the closest answer**

833 is approximately 835, which is option A. This tells us human chromosomes must use hundreds of origins of replication at once, not just one fork.

options.A: Correct. 150 million divided by (50 x 3600) gives about 833, closest to 835 forks working simultaneously.
options.B: Too high. This is roughly 150,000,000 divided by 3600, so it finds total base pairs per second but forgets to divide by the 50 base pairs per second done by each fork.
options.C: Too high. This does not match the calculation and likely comes from a mistake in converting hours to seconds or handling the zeros in 150 million.
options.D: Much too high. This is 150,000,000 divided by 50, so it forgets the time factor and assumes all the copying must happen in just 1 second instead of 1 hour.
